paragraphs: Training data attribution asks which training examples influenced a model’s prediction on a particular test example. It usually estimates what would happen if an example received more or less weight during training. This paper examines why those estimates can be unreliable for deep networks: changing the initialization or the composition of training batches can change the apparent influence.

The authors introduce a Bayesian view that treats the learned model as a posterior distribution and attribution estimates as random variables. This makes variation in influence part of the analysis. They observe that the effect of an individual training example is often smaller than the noise introduced by the training procedure.

Their experiments identify some training–test pairs whose influence persists independently of these noise sources, but such pairs are rare. The authors recommend trusting attribution explanations only in those cases. They also find disagreement between estimated and ground-truth attribution distributions, showing that representing uncertainty alone does not resolve the accuracy of the underlying influence estimates.
neurips-2023-a-bayesian-approach-to-anal.tldr: A Bayesian analysis finds that training noise often overwhelms individual-example influence, making reliable attribution rare but possible.

paragraphs: Message passing graph neural networks process both a graph and the information attached to it. Their inputs can differ in size and connectivity, making it difficult to define when two inputs are similar. This paper develops a mathematical framework for comparing these graph-and-signal inputs and using those comparisons to analyze network behavior.

The central construction is the graphon-signal cut distance. Informally, two inputs are close when they resemble samples from the same random graph-and-signal model. The distance places finite graph inputs inside a compact mathematical space, providing a common structure for comparing graphs even when their sizes and topologies differ.

The authors prove that sufficiently regular message passing networks are Lipschitz continuous in this space: changes in their outputs are controlled by changes in the input distance. They use this result to derive a generalization bound and establish stability under subsampling. The analysis allows any distribution of graph-signals, while retaining a regularity requirement on the network itself.
neurips-2023-a-graphon-signal-analysis-o.tldr: A new distance between graphs and their signals supports generalization and subsampling-stability guarantees for sufficiently regular graph neural networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning through interaction: a learner queries points and receives information about their similarity to an unknown target. The goal is to estimate that target from the responses. By expressing the interaction abstractly, the authors seek a common account of learning problems that are usually analyzed through separate mathematical frameworks.

They introduce a combinatorial measure called Dissimilarity dimension, which largely captures learnability in this setting. They also give a general algorithm whose regret and PAC generalization bounds depend polynomially on this dimension. These bounds connect a structural property of the problem to both performance during interaction and the quality of the resulting estimate.

The framework includes statistical-query learning and structured bandits as special cases. The authors explain how their dimension relates to established parameters in both areas, obtaining substantially improved analyses in some cases. The contribution is therefore both a shared language for these learning models and a way to analyze their difficulty through the same structural measure.
neurips-2023-a-unified-model-and-dimensi.tldr: Interactive estimation unifies statistical-query learning and structured bandits through a new dimension that supports polynomial learning guarantees.

paragraphs: Measuring communication between brain regions involves more than determining how much information passes between them. Researchers may also want to know what that information concerns, such as a sensory stimulus. Traditional analyses based on Wiener-Granger causality quantify overall information propagation but do not isolate the information associated with a particular feature.

The paper introduces Feature-specific Information Transfer, or FIT, to measure how much information about a chosen feature flows between two regions. It combines the directional perspective of Wiener-Granger causality with sensitivity to information content. The authors derive the measure and analytically establish its key properties, then test those properties using simulated neural activity.

In simulations, FIT separates feature-related transmission from the total information propagated between regions. Analyses of three neural datasets, covering magnetoencephalography, electroencephalography, and spiking activity, further demonstrate its ability to reveal communication content and direction beyond traditional methods. This provides a way to ask which aspects of an observed stimulus or other selected feature are being communicated.
neurips-2023-an-information-theoretic-qu.tldr: FIT measures the direction and amount of information exchanged between brain regions about a specific feature.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction returns a set of possible labels with a user-chosen coverage level. Standard coverage applies to a randomly selected test example across the population. It does not provide the stronger assurance that examples from each particular class receive that same coverage, which can matter when evaluating a classifier across many categories.

Obtaining class-specific coverage is difficult when each class has little labeled data. The proposed clustered conformal prediction method groups classes whose conformal scores are similar, then performs conformal prediction at the cluster level. This uses a grouping informed by score behavior instead of requiring each class to support an entirely separate calibration procedure.

The authors evaluate the method on four image datasets containing as many as 1,000 classes. Clustered conformal typically improves both class-conditional coverage and prediction-set size relative to existing methods. Those are complementary goals: covering the correct label is useful, but excessively large sets provide less guidance. The stated evidence is an empirical improvement on these measures, rather than an unconditional guarantee of exact coverage for every class.
neurips-2023-class-conditional-conformal.tldr: Grouping classes with similar conformal scores typically improves class-specific coverage and prediction-set size when labeled examples per class are scarce.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to draw samples from the probability distribution associated with a stochastic differential equation when its drift and diffusion are known. Its strategy is to first approximate that distribution using a positive semi-definite probability model, then draw independent, identically distributed samples from the fitted model.

The approximation is constructed by making the model satisfy the associated Fokker-Planck equation, or a fractional version, up to a chosen error. The analysis separates the cost of this preparatory calculation from the cost of producing each subsequent sample. It supplies approximation guarantees in L2 distance and, for the ordinary Fokker-Planck setting, sampling guarantees in Wasserstein-1 distance.

These results depend on smoothness of the equation’s solution and a geometric condition on its zeros. Greater smoothness improves the computational bounds; the abstract gives a particularly favorable regime when differentiability is sufficiently high relative to dimension. The findings suggest that smooth solutions can permit sampling that circumvents the curse of dimensionality without a convexity requirement. This is a conditional benefit of regularity, not a claim about every stochastic differential equation.
neurips-2023-efficient-sampling-of-stoch.tldr: Approximating SDE distributions with positive semi-definite models enables efficient independent sampling under suitable smoothness and geometric conditions.

paragraphs: Neural-network predictions can vary because of the available data and because of the training procedure itself. Training-induced noise and bias complicate uncertainty estimates, while repeatedly retraining a network can make those estimates expensive. This paper develops methods to characterize and remove procedural uncertainty in over-parameterized neural networks using neural tangent kernel theory.

The central construction is a procedural-noise-correcting predictor. It uses one auxiliary network trained on a suitably labeled dataset to remove the procedural uncertainty addressed by the framework. This gives the correction a small training requirement compared with deep ensembles, which rely on many retrained networks to assess variation.

The authors also combine the corrected predictor with computationally light resampling methods to construct confidence intervals using as few as four trained networks. Their intervals have asymptotically exact coverage, meaning the coverage guarantee is a limiting statistical statement. The contribution connects a correction for training variability with uncertainty estimates backed by theory, while keeping the number of required network trainings low.
neurips-2023-efficient-uncertainty-quant.tldr: A neural tangent kernel approach corrects procedural uncertainty with one auxiliary network and supports asymptotically exact confidence intervals with few trained networks.

paragraphs: Foundation models such as CLIP can transfer to new tasks without additional training examples, but fine-tuning and ensembling are often used to improve their performance. This paper argues that these adaptations can retain a bias inherited from pre-training: concepts that appear frequently in an imbalanced web-scale dataset receive disproportionate preference.

The authors systematically examine this label bias and propose Generalized Logit Adjustment, or GLA, to reduce it. A central difficulty is that the original pre-training data often cannot be directly inspected to measure its imbalance. GLA therefore uses an optimization-based procedure to estimate the bias and adjust the model’s prediction scores.

The reported results cover several downstream settings. GLA improves ImageNet accuracy by 1.5 percentage points, produces average gains ranging from 1.4 to 4.6 percentage points across 11 few-shot datasets, and improves long-tailed classification by 2.4 percentage points. These findings support addressing inherited label preferences as part of downstream adaptation, since fitting a model to a new task can still leave useful corrections to its existing biases.
neurips-2023-generalized-logit-adjustmen.tldr: GLA estimates and adjusts inherited label bias in foundation models, improving accuracy across several downstream classification settings.

paragraphs: A linear stochastic differential equation describes dynamics with both structured evolution and randomness. This paper asks when the distribution of the resulting process, starting from one fixed initial state, determines its generator. Identifiability matters because observational behavior must contain enough information to distinguish the underlying dynamics before those dynamics can support intervention predictions.

The authors derive different results for two forms of noise. For additive noise, they give a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for identifying the generator. For multiplicative noise, they establish a sufficient condition. The latter guarantees identification when it holds, but does not establish that identification is impossible whenever it fails.

The conditions for both settings are shown to be generic, and geometric interpretations help explain their meaning. Simulations support the theoretical findings. The causal relevance is that these identification conditions enable post-intervention distributions to be determined from the observational distribution within the linear-SDE setting. The paper therefore connects a precise mathematical identification question to the possibility of reasoning about changes to a stochastic system.
neurips-2023-generator-identification-fo.tldr: The paper establishes generator-identification conditions for linear SDEs, with a full characterization for additive noise and a sufficient condition for multiplicative noise.

paragraphs: Scene flow estimation assigns a three-dimensional motion vector to each point in a source point cloud using a target point cloud. Many leading approaches build this estimate through repeated refinement or multiple scales. GMSF instead uses a single-scale, one-shot global matching procedure, simplifying the structure of the estimation process.

The authors identify reliable feature similarity between pairs of points as essential and sufficient for accurate scene flow in their approach. They focus the model on producing these features through a hybrid local-global-cross transformer architecture. This combines several forms of feature processing to support accurate and robust representations for the global matching step.

Experiments report leading performance across multiple scene-flow benchmarks. On FlyingThings3D with occluded points, the outlier percentage falls from the previous best of 27.4% to 5.6%. The method also achieves state-of-the-art results on KITTI Scene Flow without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms previous methods on Waymo-Open. These findings support the effectiveness of improving correspondence features within a comparatively simple matching pipeline.
neurips-2023-gmsf-global-matching-scene-.tldr: GMSF estimates point-cloud motion through one-shot global matching and reports leading results using strong transformer-based correspondence features.

paragraphs: GPEX interprets neural networks by fitting Gaussian processes whose outputs closely match the networks’ outputs. Existing theoretical connections between the two often require restrictive architectures or activation functions. The paper derives an evidence lower bound that encourages this match without imposing requirements on the neural network architecture.

Making the match accurate also requires scaling Gaussian-process training. The authors introduce computational techniques that support GPU acceleration and hundreds of thousands of inducing points. In their experiments, this scale was essential for obtaining close agreement. They use ordinary ResNet-18 or feed-forward backbones with a single wide final layer, finding that only a subset of earlier theoretical assumptions was sufficient in these tests.

Across four image datasets and one biological dataset, the fitted Gaussian processes closely reproduce networks serving as classifiers or attention mechanisms. The authors then use the processes’ kernel functions to explain network decisions, providing more than 200 explanations described as highly interpretable by humans. The evidence connects output matching with a practical route to explanations through the fitted Gaussian-process model.
neurips-2023-gpex-a-framework-for-interp.tldr: GPEX fits scalable Gaussian processes to neural-network outputs and uses their kernel functions to explain the networks’ decisions.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations can learn dynamical laws from time-series observations, connecting neural networks with equation-based physical modeling. Training can be slow and produce suboptimal results, especially over longer observation periods. Architectural constraints designed to promote stable dynamics can also be unsuitable when the unknown governing equation may not satisfy those constraints.

This paper changes the training method without requiring changes to the model architecture. It combines synchronization, which brings model dynamics into alignment with the training data, with homotopy optimization. The authors show that synchronization makes the originally irregular loss landscape more manageable, creating a setting that the homotopy procedure can use to improve training.

Benchmark experiments find competitive or better training loss while often using fewer than half as many training epochs as other model-agnostic techniques. The trained models also show improved extrapolation. Together, these findings suggest that shaping the optimization process can help dynamics discovery without requiring the architecture to encode stability assumptions that may be inappropriate for the system being learned.
neurips-2023-homotopy-based-training-of-.tldr: Synchronization and homotopy optimization improve NeuralODE training and extrapolation without changing the model architecture.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a data-rich source setting to a target setting with fewer resources. One common approach aligns feature distributions across the two domains. This paper examines how that idea should work for ranking, where examples are organized into lists and performance is evaluated through the ordering within those lists.

The authors find that earlier ranking approaches typically align individual items pooled across all lists. This ignores the grouping that defines the ranking task. They propose aligning representations at the list level instead, so the domain-invariance objective reflects the structure on which both the data and ranking metrics depend.

The resulting analysis provides what the authors describe as the first domain-adaptation generalization bound for ranking, giving theoretical support to list-level alignment. Experiments also show better transfer in unsupervised domain adaptation for ranking tasks, including passage reranking. The contribution links the unit being aligned to the unit being evaluated: preserving list structure becomes part of both the method and its theoretical justification.
neurips-2023-learning-list-level-domain-.tldr: Aligning whole-list representations across domains gives ranking-specific theoretical support and improves empirical transfer performance.

paragraphs: Open-set fine-grained retrieval must find relevant images from categories that were absent during training. Visual attributes learned from known categories can provide a way to represent those unfamiliar categories. However, explicitly labeling attributes is labor-intensive. This paper asks how a retrieval model trained with image-level supervision can acquire useful attribute representations without those annotations.

The proposed Visual Attribute Parameterization Network, or VAPNet, extracts detailed semantic information from local image patches and distills visual attributes from it. During training, it repeatedly refines the attributes to improve their quality. Those attributes also serve as supervisory signals for tuning the retrieval model, embedding the attribute knowledge into its parameters.

The intended result is a model that can extract and use visual attributes when representing unknown categories. Experiments on open-set fine-grained retrieval datasets report better performance than existing solutions. This supports the approach of learning transferable attribute information from category-supervised images, while avoiding a separate requirement for manually annotated attributes during training.
neurips-2023-learning-to-parameterize-vi.tldr: VAPNet learns and refines visual attributes without attribute annotations to improve retrieval for categories unseen during training.

paragraphs: Machine-learning models for molecular properties are often evaluated on standardized benchmarks, but those evaluations may differ from the situations encountered in drug discovery. This paper argues that existing benchmarks can therefore give an overly optimistic picture of practical performance. It introduces Lo-Hi to connect evaluation more closely to the drug-discovery process.

The benchmark contains two tasks, Lead Optimization and Hit Identification. For Hit Identification, the authors design a molecular data-splitting algorithm that solves a Balanced Vertex Minimum k-Cut problem. This makes the construction of the evaluation split a central part of the benchmark’s approach to representing a practical discovery setting.

The authors test both contemporary state-of-the-art methods and classic machine-learning models to examine which perform better under these settings. They also analyze existing benchmarks and report that they are unrealistic and overoptimistic. The contribution is a revised basis for model comparison: judging molecular-property predictors on tasks shaped around intended use, rather than treating strong results on an existing benchmark as sufficient evidence of practical effectiveness.
neurips-2023-lo-hi-practical-ml-drug-dis.tldr: Lo-Hi evaluates molecular-property models on lead optimization and hit identification tasks designed to better reflect practical drug discovery.

paragraphs: Conditional image repainting can produce unrealistic lighting, making the repainted content inconsistent with its surroundings. LuminAIRe introduces an illumination-aware version of this task. The approach explicitly incorporates estimates of the scene’s lighting and three-dimensional geometry into image generation so that the foreground and background can have harmonized lighting effects.

The method begins with a background image and parsing masks. It estimates environmental lighting and geometry using a parametric lighting representation together with learned priors. A physically based illumination-rendering process and an illumination attention module then turn those estimates into illumination images. These images supply lighting information to the generation process.

Experiments report superior results to state-of-the-art conditional repainting methods, supporting the value of making illumination an explicit condition for generation. The authors also collect Car-LuminAIRe, a dataset with lighting annotations and varied appearances, to support development and evaluation of the task. The work combines a lighting-aware generation pipeline with data intended to make lighting realism a directly studied part of repainting.
neurips-2023-luminaire-illumination-awar.tldr: LuminAIRe uses estimated lighting and geometry to guide image repainting toward consistent foreground and background illumination.

paragraphs: Robotic perception needs to describe both the shape of a scene and what its contents mean. Three-dimensional bounding boxes provide limited geometric detail and struggle with objects outside a predefined vocabulary. Occupancy prediction instead estimates detailed occupied-space states and their semantics, motivating datasets that support this richer description of the environment.

Occ3D introduces a pipeline for generating dense labels that account for visibility. Its three stages are voxel densification, occlusion reasoning, and refinement guided by images. Together, these stages address how to construct detailed scene labels while reasoning about which parts of the environment are visible or obscured.

The authors use the pipeline to establish Occ3D-Waymo and Occ3D-nuScenes from the corresponding driving datasets. They analyze performance with several baseline models and introduce a Coarse-to-Fine Occupancy network, CTF-Occ, which performs better on the proposed benchmarks. The contribution includes both the infrastructure for evaluating detailed occupancy prediction and a model demonstrating improved results within that evaluation setting.
neurips-2023-occ3d-a-large-scale-3d-occu.tldr: Occ3D provides dense, visibility-aware occupancy benchmarks and a coarse-to-fine model for detailed three-dimensional driving-scene perception.

paragraphs: This paper studies two-layer fully connected networks with linear activations, trained by gradient flow on squared loss. Even in this simplified setting, optimization can favor particular parameter structures. The authors examine how that implicit preference depends on the scale of the initial weights, connecting initialization to the solution eventually reached.

Their main result characterizes the loss minimizers selected by gradient flow for a specific initialization shape through a variational formulation. In the regime of small initialization scale, this characterization reveals a preference for a low-rank hidden-layer structure. Thus, the parameterization and training dynamics can favor a restricted internal representation without adding an explicit low-rank objective.

The authors also identify a hidden mirror flow that tracks the singular values of the weight matrices and describes how they evolve over time. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical phenomena. These results explain a concrete form of optimization bias within the stated linear-network setting, with the initialization shape and scale playing explicit roles in the analysis.
neurips-2023-on-the-spectral-bias-of-two.tldr: For a specified initialization shape, small-scale initialization biases gradient-flow training of two-layer linear networks toward low-rank hidden representations.

paragraphs: A supervised pre-training dataset can contain many classes, many examples within each class, or some balance between the two. With a fixed total number of examples, increasing one kind of diversity reduces room for the other. This paper studies how that allocation affects performance on tasks learned after pre-training.

The experiments find that downstream performance is best when the two forms of diversity are balanced. The theory shows that performance depends monotonically on both forms, explaining why the fixed-size constraint creates a meaningful trade-off. It also reveals that the optimal ratio of class count to examples per class is invariant to total dataset size within the theoretical analysis.

That result motivates a method for predicting how many pre-training classes to use. Applied with ImageNet as the pre-training dataset, the method improves downstream performance by around two points. The paper therefore connects dataset composition to transfer quality and uses its theoretical account to guide a concrete choice about how a pre-training dataset should be organized.
neurips-2023-on-the-trade-off-of-intra-i.tldr: Balancing class count and examples per class improves supervised pre-training, and a theoretical ratio helps predict a useful class count.

paragraphs: Private synthetic-data generators may produce useful datasets without knowing the requirements of a particular downstream task. A user can nevertheless need certain measures to be well represented, and failing those requirements can reduce the dataset’s usefulness. This paper introduces a post-processing method that adapts generated data to measures chosen by the user.

The method resamples the synthetic dataset, filtering out samples that do not meet the selected utility measures. It finds optimal resampling weights with an efficient stochastic first-order algorithm. Those weights determine how the existing synthetic samples contribute to the resulting dataset, making the user’s priorities part of the post-processing procedure.

The authors report that this adjustment preserves strong privacy guarantees and dataset quality while improving the chosen utility measures. Numerical experiments show consistent improvements across multiple benchmark datasets and state-of-the-art synthetic-data generators. The result gives downstream users a way to tailor an already generated private dataset to their requirements, with the reported benefits tied to the measures selected for improvement.
neurips-2023-post-processing-private-syn.tldr: Optimized resampling improves private synthetic data on user-selected utility measures while preserving privacy guarantees and dataset quality.

paragraphs: Models that predict the effects of protein mutations are difficult to compare when studies use different datasets and performance varies across protein families. ProteinGym addresses this evaluation problem through a large, standardized collection of tasks for protein fitness prediction and design. Its goal is to make comparisons broader and more consistent.

ProteinGym v1.0 includes more than 250 standardized deep mutational scanning assays covering millions of mutated sequences. It also contains curated clinical datasets with expert annotations of mutation effects. The evaluation framework combines prediction and design metrics, accounts for known limitations of the experimental methods, and includes both zero-shot and supervised settings.

The authors evaluate more than 40 high-performing models from multiple areas, including mutation-effect prediction and inverse folding. They release the datasets, code, sequence alignments, structures, and predictions, alongside a website for comparison. The contribution is a common evaluation foundation across many proteins and settings, helping researchers assess model effectiveness beyond results on a small or individually selected collection of experiments.
neurips-2023-proteingym-large-scale-benc.tldr: ProteinGym standardizes large-scale evaluation of protein mutation prediction and design across diverse assays, clinical data, models, and learning settings.

paragraphs: In contextual batched bandits, rewards arrive together at the end of an episode, and only rewards for actions actually taken are observed. This leaves the learner with partial feedback. The paper proposes Sketched Policy Updating with Imputed Rewards, or SPUIR, to estimate missing rewards and approximate the information that fuller feedback would provide.

The method formulates reward completion as an imputation-regularized ridge regression problem that represents feedback from executed and non-executed actions. Randomized sketching reduces the cost of solving that regression. The missing rewards are therefore model-based estimates, incorporated into policy updating through a computationally efficient optimization procedure.

The analysis establishes instantaneous regret with controllable bias and lower variance than approaches without imputation, as well as a sublinear regret bound relative to the optimal policy. The authors add rate-scheduled and nonlinear-reward extensions. Experiments on synthetic, public benchmark, and real-world datasets report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting the practical value of the proposed bias–variance trade-off and computational approach.
neurips-2023-reward-imputation-with-sket.tldr: SPUIR combines reward imputation with randomized sketching to improve batched-bandit learning with controllable bias, reduced variance, and sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Clustering large datasets becomes expensive when runtime multiplies the number of data points, dimensions, and requested clusters. This paper introduces a randomized algorithm based on one-dimensional projections whose expected runtime is O(nnz(X) + n log n). Here, nnz(X) counts nonzero entries, so sparse inputs can make the data-processing cost particularly favorable.

The theoretical analysis shows how an approximation obtained after a random one-dimensional projection can be transferred back to the original points. It also establishes an expected O(n log n) implementation of k-means++ seeding in one dimension. The complete algorithm has a worst-case approximation ratio of roughly k to the fourth power, up to suppressed logarithmic factors.

Experiments generally produce substantially better cluster quality than that worst-case guarantee suggests. The authors evaluate both direct k-means clustering and coreset construction, reporting a new trade-off between speed and quality relative to earlier methods. The appeal is the removal of a multiplicative cluster-count factor from the stated expected runtime, while retaining a provable, though comparatively loose, approximation guarantee.
neurips-2023-simple-scalable-and-effecti.tldr: Random one-dimensional projections enable clustering with fast expected runtime and a provable approximation bound, with stronger quality observed empirically.

paragraphs: Streaming principal component analysis estimates a leading direction of variation while processing observations sequentially. Oja’s algorithm is an established method for this task, but much of its convergence theory assumes independent samples. This paper analyzes the more dependent setting in which observations are generated by a Markov chain.

The target is the top eigenvector of the covariance matrix of the chain’s stationary distribution. The analysis assumes an irreducible, aperiodic, reversible chain that starts in stationarity. Such a setting is relevant when observations can only be obtained through a Markov Chain Monte Carlo procedure and the desired inference concerns its stationary distribution.

A common response to dependence is to discard observations until the retained stream is nearly independent. The authors instead establish a near-optimal convergence rate for Oja’s algorithm using the entire stream. Their result removes the logarithmic dependence on sample size associated with those downsampling strategies. Under the stated chain assumptions, this provides theoretical support for retaining dependent observations when estimating the principal direction.
neurips-2023-streaming-pca-for-markovian.tldr: For specified stationary Markov chains, Oja’s algorithm achieves a near-optimal streaming PCA rate without discarding observations to approximate independence.

paragraphs: Graph-based self-supervised methods commonly emphasize pairwise relationships. This can overlook higher-order interactions and long-range dependencies needed to represent topology. TopoSRL develops self-supervised learning for simplicial complexes, seeking representations that retain both these richer interactions and the local and global structure of the input.

The method introduces a simplicial augmentation procedure that efficiently creates two views of a complex. It then applies a new contrastive loss to the generated simplices. The augmentation provides the views used for learning, while the loss is designed to preserve local and global information in the representations. Together, these components adapt the learning objective to simplicial structure.

Experiments across several datasets report better performance than state-of-the-art graph self-supervised methods and supervised simplicial neural models. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed approach for learning from simplicial-complex data without task-label supervision. The paper’s contribution is a coordinated choice of data augmentation and contrastive objective aimed at retaining topology while learning representations of higher-order relationships.
neurips-2023-toposrl-topology-preserving.tldr: TopoSRL uses simplicial augmentation and contrastive learning to preserve topology and capture higher-order interactions in self-supervised representations.
